Associated People: Xuanzang; Yijing; Atisha; unnamed Pala-period monks
Associated Object (fill out itinerant ob: Terracotta lotus tile (Nalanda); miniature bronze votive stupas
Other Historical Facts: Major point of origin for monks travelling to Southeast Asia; documented in Chinese pilgrimage accounts
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Nalanda served as the primary point of departure for Buddhist monks travelling overland and by sea toward Southeast Asia between the 5th and 12th centuries. Chinese pilgrims' accounts and the distribution of material culture—particularly terracotta lotus tiles and bronze votive objects—confirm that Nalanda-trained monks carried not only texts and ideas but also aesthetic conventions, including the ubiquitous lotus motif, to monasteries as far as Sriksetra (Myanmar), Paharpur (Bangladesh), and ultimately Java. The route from Nalanda to the eastern coast of India, specifically the ports of the Krishna-Guntur delta (near Amaravati), formed the first stage of the maritime passage to Southeast Asia. Monks departed with portable religious objects—miniature stupas, bronze images, clay tablets with lotus-throne Buddhas—that served both as personal devotional items and as gifts to newly established monasteries abroad. This material mobility was critical to the visual homogenisation of Buddhist sacred space across Monsoon Asia.
References: Sen, Tansen. Buddhism, Diplomacy, and Trade. Honolulu: UHP, 2003. | Ray, Himanshu Prabha. The Winds of Change. Delhi: OUP, 1994. | Liu, Xinru. The Silk Road in World History. Oxford: OUP, 2010.
Further Readings: Schopen, Gregory. Bones, Stones, and Buddhist Monks. Honolulu: UHP, 1997.

Place Name: Krishna-Guntur delta / Amaravati port region, Andhra Pradesh
Associated People: Unnamed merchant monks; Sātavāhana and later Pallava donors
Associated Object (fill out itinerant ob: Stone relief panel with lotus pond (Amaravati); Lotus medallion gold coin
Other Historical Facts: Key embarkation point for Bay of Bengal maritime routes; home of the Amaravati sculptural school
Analytical Description (150-250 words): The Krishna-Guntur coastal delta, home to the great stupa at Amaravati and several nearby port towns, was a pivotal embarkation zone for Buddhist missionaries and traders crossing the Bay of Bengal to Southeast Asia. The Amaravati sculptural school, active from approximately the 2nd century BCE to the 4th century CE, developed a highly influential visual vocabulary—including the lotus pond scene—that was systematically adopted by early Buddhist monuments in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, and Java. Archaeological evidence from coastal sites in this region includes finds of Roman amphorae, Southeast Asian ceramics, and gold coins with lotus emblems, attesting to the multi-directional nature of maritime exchange. The lotus motif, central to Amaravati's iconographic programme, thus functioned as a portable visual currency, legible to Buddhist communities across the entire arc of the Indian Ocean. Monks and merchants departing from these ports carried both objects and the visual templates inscribed on them, seeding new iconographic programmes at their destinations.
References: Knox, Robert. Amaravati: Buddhist Sculpture from the Great Stupa. London: BMP, 1992. | Wicks, Robert S. Money, Markets, and Trade in Early Southeast Asia. Ithaca: Cornell, 1992. | Ray, Himanshu Prabha. The Archaeology of Seafaring in Ancient South Asia. Cambridge: CUP, 2003.
Further Readings: Begley, Vimala and Richard Daniel De Puma, eds. Rome and India: The Ancient Sea Trade. Madison: UWP, 1991.

Associated People: Rajendra I (Chola); Tamil merchant guilds (Ayyavole, Manigramam)
Associated Object (fill out itinerant ob: Standing Buddha (Tamil Nadu); Ayyavole Merchant Guild Stone Inscription
Other Historical Facts: Site of the Chudamani Vihara Buddhist monastery; major Chola port facing the Bay of Bengal; departure point for the 1025 CE naval expedition against Srivijaya.
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Nagapattinam was the most cosmopolitan religious site on the Coromandel Coast during the first millennium CE. Simultaneously a major Shaiva pilgrimage centre, a Buddhist hub with a working monastery endowed by Srivijayan royal patronage, and the primary departure point for Tamil merchant guilds whose inscribed stones have been found from Kerala to Quanzhou. John Guy has documented the dense web of relationships between Nagapattinam's Buddhist workshops, Chola royal patronage, and Srivijayan maritime networks, revealing a port city in which religious, commercial, and diplomatic exchanges were inseparable. The Chudamani Vihara (Jewel-Crest Monastery), endowed by the Srivijayan king Maravijayottungavarman with Rajaraja I's permission, physically embodied this entanglement. When Rajendra I launched his naval raid on Srivijaya in 1025 CE, Nagapattinam served as the fleet's assembly and departure point, illuminating how commercial, religious, and military circuits overlapped in the medieval Indian Ocean world.
References: Guy, John. "The Lost Temples of Nagapattinam and Quanzhou." Orientations 25, no. 7 (1994). | Guy, John. "Tamil Merchants and the Hindu-Buddhist Diaspora." In Early Interactions. Singapore: ISEAS, 2011. | Kulke, Hermann et al., eds. Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa. Singapore: ISEAS, 2009.
Further Readings: Ahilan, Karuppiah. "Political Boundaries or Cultural Zones." (2017).

Associated People: Rajendra I; Rajaraja I; Chola governors; Sri Lankan Buddhist sangha
Associated Object (fill out itinerant ob: Clay dharani tablet with lotus-throne Buddha
Other Historical Facts: Sri Lanka conquered by Rajaraja I in 1017 CE; Polonnaruwa made Chola capital; Tamil Shaiva temples constructed alongside existing Buddhist infrastructure; Vijayabahu I expelled the Cholas in 1070 CE.
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Sri Lanka occupied a pivotal position in the medieval Indian Ocean network, functioning simultaneously as a major Buddhist pilgrimage destination, a critical waystop on the Bay of Bengal sea route, and a contested political prize between South Indian powers. The Chola conquest under Rajaraja I in 1017 CE installed a Tamil-speaking administration that coexisted uneasily with the island's Theravada Buddhist institutions. Chola governors constructed Tamil Shaiva temples at Polonnaruwa while also patronising Buddhist monuments, a dual strategy mirroring the religious pragmatism of Tamil merchant guilds documented by John Guy across Southeast Asia. The island's port cities, particularly Mantai on the north coast, were ancient nodes in the Bay of Bengal trade network. Portable Buddhist objects including clay dharani tablets, bronze votive images, and miniature stupas moved in both directions through these ports, embedding Sri Lankan and South Indian Buddhist visual cultures within a shared iconographic field.
References: Bandaranayake, Senake. "Sri Lanka and Monsoon Asia." In Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa. Singapore: ISEAS, 2009. | Ray, Himanshu Prabha. The Winds of Change. Delhi: OUP, 1994.
Further Readings: Brancaccio, Pia. "Monumental Rock-cut Images from Sri Lanka: New Perspectives."

Associated People: Rajendra I (attacker); local Malay rulers; Tamil merchant communities
Associated Object (fill out itinerant ob: Ayyavole Merchant Guild Stone Inscription; Bronze Vajra
Other Historical Facts: Named in Rajendra I's Tanjore victory inscription as a primary raid target; controlled the northern Strait of Malacca; Tamil merchant guild inscriptions and Hindu-Buddhist temples survive at Bujang Valley.
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Kadaram, identified with the Bujang Valley area of modern Kedah, is one of the principal targets named in Rajendra I's victory inscription of 1025 CE. The Bujang Valley archaeological record reveals Hindu-Buddhist temple complexes active from the 5th to the 14th century CE, making this one of the earliest continuously occupied Indic religious sites in the Malay world. Tamil merchant guild inscriptions, bronze icons, and Indian-style brick temples attest to the sustained presence of South Indian commercial and religious networks at this strategic location. Kadaram controlled the northern mouth of the Strait of Malacca, and its submission was as much a commercial as a military objective for Rajendra I. The Chola raid did not establish permanent occupation; rather, it functioned as a demonstration of naval reach intended to redirect Strait of Malacca trade toward Chola-aligned networks and away from Srivijayan control.

Further Readings: Andaya, Barbara Watson. "Seas, Oceans and Cosmologies in Southeast Asia." (2017).

Associated People: Rajendra I; Srivijayan king Sangrama Vijayottungavarman; Chinese pilgrim Yijing (671-695 CE)
Other Historical Facts: Capital of the Srivijayan maritime empire; Yijing stopped here for years to study Sanskrit; struck by Rajendra I's 1025 CE naval expedition; Srivijayan power declined thereafter.
Analytical Description (150-250 words): Palembang in South Sumatra was the heartland of the Srivijayan maritime empire, which dominated the Strait of Malacca and Bay of Bengal trade from the 7th to the 13th century CE. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing, who stopped at Srivijaya in 671 CE on his way to Nalanda, described a thriving Buddhist community of over a thousand monks engaged in Sanskrit learning, making the city an intermediary station between Chinese and Indian Buddhist scholarship. Srivijayan kings aggressively patronised South Asian Buddhist institutions, including Nalanda in Bihar and the Chudamani Vihara at Nagapattinam, creating material and institutional links moving objects, texts, and ideas across the Bay of Bengal. The 1025 CE Chola naval raid disrupted but did not destroy this network; Srivijayan maritime power gradually declined thereafter, with Chola-aligned Tamil merchant guilds increasingly dominant in the Strait's commercial life.

Further Readings: Acri, Andrea. "The Place of Nusantara in the Sanskritic Buddhist Cosmopolis." (2018).
